title: Which was the original 'football'? | SPORTS WORDS

entries.note: Short for [[from:disport]] and once meant any pastime; its meaning has since fallen in line with Latin [[see:ludus]], a game or play.
To carry someone away from what they normally do, with the port of [[same-root:transport]]; Chaucer used it in 1386, and it gave [[gave:sport]].
Its port is the same element as in [[same-root:disport]], which shows the idea of carrying something away.
A salesperson, explained through Chaucer's line about going to Rome for chapmanhood or for [[see:disport]].
Compared with [[see:disport]]: the same idea of something that diverts your attention.
Latin word for a game or play; [[see:sport]] has come to mean much the same, and ludus gave [[gave:ludicrous]].
From Latin [[from:ludus]]; it first meant to do with a sport or game, and now figuratively means ridiculous, as if it were all a game.
In the same group as [[see:ludicrous]], because it is related to the word [[from:fable]].
A vague term, used since at least the 1400s, for games of getting a ball to a goal; banned in Scotland in 1424 and condemned in 1531 as beastly fury.
Originally a line or destination rather than a net or frame, as its etymology shows.
A brutal game played around Shrove Tuesday in Ashbourne, Derbyshire, where players fight to move a huge ball from one river to another.
Originally a reference to hunting.
Originally rugby football: football played in the style of [[from:Rugby School]]; the oval ball only became a rule in the 1890s.
Boarding school in Warwickshire whose style of football gave [[gave:rugby]] its name.
Not an Americanism: formed at Oxford University from association, for the game played under [[from:Football Association]] rules; Rob finds it more precise than [[see:football]].
Body set up in Britain in the 1870s or 1880s to organise the first leagues; its name gave [[gave:soccer]].
Oxford University shortening of rugby football, paired with [[see:soccer]] for association football.
Oxford University shortening that Rob thinks referred to a boat in one of the boat races, alongside [[see:soccer]] and [[see:rugger]].
An alternative name for soccer that is older than [[see:soccer]]; nobody uses it now, and saying it would sound like trying too hard.
The very common British name for football, unlike the unused [[see:footer]].
An early, inconsistently used name for American football, because the lines on the field look like a cooking [[from:gridiron]].
Early American college games played under rules closer to association football, part of the story of [[see:gridiron football]].
A two-game series that brought rugby-style handling into US colleges and helped set [[see:gridiron football]] apart from association and rugby football.
Named after the [[from:Northern Rugby Football League]]; played with 13 players and a six-tackle rule, and more popular in the north of England.
Based on the rules of the [[from:Rugby Football Union]]; amateur until 1995, with 15 players and five points for a try, unlike [[see:rugby league]].
Once worth no points: scoring one only earned the chance to try for points with the [[see:conversion]]; now worth four or five points.
Kicking the ball through the posts after a [[see:try]], which used to be the only way to score points; American football took the term from rugby.
One of the American football terms taken from rugby, though Rob hasn't heard it used in modern rugby.
Another American football term that Jess says was taken straight from rugby, like [[see:touchdown]].
Rugby name for the lines at the side of the pitch, not at the end.
The invisible line where each American football play begins, from the earlier rugby term [[from:scrummage]].
Earlier rugby term, a 15th-century variant of [[from:skirmish]], for players packed together fighting for the ball; it gave [[gave:line of scrimmage]].
Rugby formation of tightly packed players, short for [[from:scrummage]]; so a scrum is really a skirmish, a little battle.
American football term that sounds naughty if you're only half listening, noted down by Jess while watching NFL games.

Became standard corporate language through American football; first cited in 1939 in the Los Angeles Times, about a game involving the Bruins.
Originally books of theatrical plays; it only became a corporate term after American football brought it in.
In American football, a tactic for a specific set piece, as collected in a [[see:playbook]].
An American football idiom that has entered everyday language.
An American football term now used figuratively, as in punting decisions to somebody else.
An American football idiom that has entered everyday language.
An American football idiom that has entered everyday language.
Listed as an American football idiom, though Jess admits it could come from a number of sports.
Running a blitz, or a media blitz, was mostly unheard of until American football started using it.
In American football, a change made at the line after reading the defence; figuratively, a change of plan in response to new information.
Jess lists it as an American football idiom, Rob claims it for soccer; Jess agrees, though American football made the figurative use popular in corporate settings.
Origin uncertain: probably from an earlier English cricket meaning stool, less likely Old English [[from?:cricc]]; not from French [[unrelated:criquet]], and unrelated to the insect.
A sport older than [[see:cricket]] and mostly played by women, in which you guarded an actual stool; it supports the stool theory for cricket.
Old English noun meaning a crutch, almost certainly the source of [[gave:crutch]]; etymologists doubt it gave [[gave?:cricket]] because of the sound change.
Not related to [[unrelated:cricket]]; a much later sport that reached England via Ireland in the 19th century, from a dialect form of [[from:crochet]].
Refers to the little hooks you crochet with, which suits threading the ball through hoops; source of [[gave:croquet]] and related to [[same-root:lacrosse]].
Not playing by the rules or in the right spirit; first said by cricket players about the game itself, as in an 1867 quote, then applied to everyday life.
Same word as the small door in a big castle door or gate, from Norman French [[from:wiket]], which also gave French [[same-root:guichet]].
Modern French form of the word behind [[same-root:wicket]], meaning a ticket office or toll booth.
A cricket idiom; Rob confirms that people really do talk about playing on a sticky [[see:wicket]].
To be astounded or overwhelmed, from hitting a cricket ball over the boundary without it touching the ground, which scores six runs.
Would be a lesser shock than [[see:hit for six]], since a ball that bounces before the boundary scores four, but nobody says it.
An Indigenous game; the name is from French [[from:la crosse]], the stick, as [[see:Jean de Brébeuf]] called it in 1637, likening the sticks to a bishop's [[see:crosier]].
Jesuit missionary said to have first written down the name [[see:lacrosse]] in 1637, describing the Huron people playing a stick-and-ball game.
Iroquois name for the game that became [[equivalent:lacrosse]], referring to the bodily contact of its originally high-contact forms.
Ojibwe name for the game that became [[equivalent:lacrosse]], similar in meaning to the Iroquois [[equivalent:dehontsigwaehs]].
Mohawk term for the game that became [[equivalent:lacrosse]].
Choctaw name for the game that became [[equivalent:lacrosse]], and Jess's favourite of the Indigenous names.
From French [[from:billard]], a small stick, with the diminutive -ard ending; one of many sports named after a stick, like [[see:lacrosse]].
Combines [[from:black pool]] and [[from:pyramids]]; invented in British India, where [[see:Sir Neville Chamberlain]] used army slang for a green recruit, snooker, for a poor player.
A game where coloured balls had to be potted in a set order; one of the two games combined into [[see:snooker]].
A game played with a triangle of balls; combined with [[see:black pool]] to make [[see:snooker]].
Army colonel, not the later prime minister, said to have named [[see:snooker]] while playing in Jabalpur with the Devonshire Regiment.
Named after the pool meaning the pot: the combined stakes or prize; [[see:snooker]] was originally called snooker's pool.
Scottish word probably meaning to strike or cuff, from a root meaning club or bat; related to Germanic words for bell clappers and maces, and banned 1400s–1600s.
Scottish king whose acts banned [[see:golf]] as an unprofitable sport, yet he bought his own golf balls and clubs in 1502.
Apparently played [[see:golf]] quite a bit, and [[see:pall-mall]] too.
A lawn game also played by [[see:Mary, Queen of Scots]], pronounced differently depending on who you talk to.
Related to [[same-root:pair]] and meaning equal: making par means equalling the ideal player.
Now one over par but originally par itself, after [[see:Major Wellman]] called the notional opponent a regular [[from:bogeyman]] in 1890; later meant an average competent player.
Golfer who in an 1890 game, thinking of a popular song, called the invincible notional opponent a regular bogeyman, giving [[gave:bogey]].
One under par, from the earlier [[from:bird]], meaning something excellent; [[see:eagle]], [[see:albatross]] and [[see:condor]] follow as bigger feats.
Golf score named after a bird, following [[see:birdie]], with bigger birds for bigger feats.
Golf score named after a bird, following [[see:birdie]], with bigger birds for bigger feats.
Golf score named after a bird, following [[see:birdie]], with bigger birds for bigger feats.
The earlier word for one under par, from bird meaning something really clever or good; it gave [[gave:birdie]].
From French [[from:cadet]], a junior person, which was pronounced much like caddie.
What you shout when a ball goes astray; short for [[from:fore-caddie]], the spotter ahead on the hole, meaning look out in front.
A golf idiom used in other contexts, based on [[see:par]].
A golf idiom used in other contexts, based on [[see:par]].
A golf idiom used in other contexts.
In golf, an informal second chance off the tee, now used figuratively, as in taking a mulligan on a project; its origin stories are confusing.
First recorded in England in 1744, in a pocketbook published by John Newbery; the first recorded game, in Surrey in 1749, featured the future [[see:George III]].
As Prince of Wales, played in the first recorded game of [[see:baseball]], in Surrey in 1749.
British school game similar to [[see:baseball]], played with a smaller one-handed bat; it lasted in America until baseball was codified.
Spelling, as in basting a turkey, in the first American reference to [[see:baseball]], a Princeton student's diary; probably an eggcorn.
Another name for [[see:baseball]] used in New York and the Great Lakes region until the early 19th century.
Another name for [[see:baseball]] used in New York and the Great Lakes region until the early 19th century.
Took the Gotham Club's rules and founded the [[see:Knickerbocker Base Ball Club]].
Early New York baseball club founded by [[see:Alexander Cartwright]], named after the Knickerbocker Fire Engine Company.
Discussed in an earlier episode; common in New York history thanks to [[from:Washington Irving]]'s satirical character [[from:Diedrich Knickerbocker]].
Washington Irving's character and pen name, whose distinctive trousers, baggy around the knee, became baseball pants.
Derby County's stadium for most of its history, named because it was the centre of a failed attempt to introduce baseball to England.
Suffix for football teams formed when several teams merged into one, as with [[see:Manchester United]].
Fans protesting the club's ownership wore red and green scarves as a nod to the precursor clubs that merged to form it.
Suffix for clubs without a ground of their own, which had to wander between venues, like Bolton Wanderers.
Suffix for clubs that, like [[see:Wanderers]], had no ground and had to rove, like Bristol Rovers.
Suffix Rob thinks refers to clubs picking players from a broad geographical range, as with Glasgow Rangers.
Suffix for clubs that grew out of athletics clubs, like Oldham Athletic.
A word for Britain, used as a grand, patriotic name for clubs like West Bromwich Albion.

A British idiom Rob thinks may come from rugby, where [[see:touch]] is the side line, rather than from football.
Invented in 1891 by [[see:James Naismith]]; [[see:Frank Mahan]] suggested the name because they had a basket and a ball, after [[see:Naismith ball]] was rejected.
Canadian-American YMCA instructor who invented [[see:basketball]] in 1891 with a soccer ball and two peach baskets to keep students busy in winter.
Player in the first game who insisted it needed a name, proposed [[see:Naismith ball]], then suggested [[see:basketball]].
Name first proposed for [[see:basketball]]; [[see:James Naismith]] laughed and said it would kill any game.
Like [[see:basketball]] without bouncing or a backboard; players stay still, only the goal attack and goal shooter can score, and Rob wonders which came first.
One of the few football idioms Rob finds; a football phenomenon that is hard to achieve in many other sports.
Football tactic of putting all your defenders behind the ball; now used figuratively to mean playing it ultra safe.
Not letting in any goals, though it sounds like it could be an idiom about not soiling the bed.
Basketball term now used outside the sport, from the French acrobatic exclamation [[from:allez-hop]], let's go up.
Basketball term Jess lists alongside [[see:alley-oop]] among those used outside the game.

Coined by [[from:Alex Ferguson]] for the tense end of a match; now a British phrase for tense moments, its exact sense unclear, perhaps clenching.
Highly successful Manchester United manager who called the tense end of a match [[gave:squeaky bum time]].
